title: What are gargoyles? Monsters with a rainy-day job
description: A gargoyle does more than pull a face: it sends rainwater away from a building. Discover the difference between a gargoyle and a grotesque.

cover.alt: An imaginary stone creature on a Gothic ledge pours rainwater from its open mouth away from the wall
cover.credit: AI-generated conceptual illustration created for BrainiLab; not a photograph or reconstruction of a named cathedral or sculpture.

practice: Try the History Quiz for more stories behind familiar sights.

sections.title: A monster with a practical job
sections.html:
A gargoyle is a carved waterspout that carries rainwater away from a building’s walls. Its startling face may get your attention, but its plumbing gives it the job title.

Historic England’s archive exhibition shows creatures and human figures doing this work. The name comes from the Old French gargouille, meaning throat.

sections.title: Why stick your neck out?
sections.html:
A projecting spout sends water out into the air instead of letting it run down the masonry. Washington National Cathedral explains how its gargoyles protect the stone.

The long mouth makes more sense once you imagine a rainy day. Another building detail worth a closer look is the little lumps in Roman concrete.

sections.title: Gargoyle or grotesque? Follow the water
sections.html:
A carved creature without a working waterspout is generally called a grotesque. Looking alarming is not enough to make it a gargoyle.

That is the useful distinction when two figures seem equally monstrous: one channels roof water through a spout; the other does not. You need to inspect the function as well as the face.

sections.title: Even Darth Vader has a place
sections.html:
Washington National Cathedral has a Darth Vader grotesque on its northwest tower. Its own account traces the design to a children’s competition in the 1980s. Gothic style does not automatically mean medieval age.

Appearances can tell a misleading story. Those familiar horned Viking helmets offer another good reason to look twice.
